examples: When adding file upload to a council's planning portal, you spot the risk of malicious files and suggest virus scanning and file-type checks before it goes to review.
In a pull request you notice secrets in a config file, explain why they belong in the secrets manager, and point to the fix.
actions: Run a lightweight threat model on the feature you're building and share it with your tech lead.
Check your current codebase against three of the OWASP Top 10 risks.
obj: When we added file upload to the planning portal, I flagged the risk of malicious files and added virus scanning and file-type checks. It passed the security review first time.

examples: You take the architect's logical design for a booking service and turn it into a physical one: which services, which database, how they talk, documented in the repo.
Before building a new notification feature you write a short design doc with a sequence diagram and get two engineers to review it.
actions: Write a one-page design doc for your next story that's bigger than three days, and ask a senior engineer to review it.
Document one existing component using the C4 model.
obj: I took the architect's logical design for the booking service and chose the services, database and queues to build it, then got it signed off before coding.
I wrote a detailed design for the notifications feature, with data flows and error handling, which the team built from with no major rework.
I documented the payments integration in the repo using C4 diagrams and an architecture decision record, so a new joiner could pick it up in a day.
I designed the reporting export to run off a read replica, keeping risk to the live service low while still meeting the client's monthly reporting need.
I chose a standard queue-and-worker pattern for bulk emails instead of something bespoke, which kept it simple and easy for the client's team to support.

examples: At show and tell you explain an API change in terms of what caseworkers will see, not which endpoints moved.
You notice the designer's prototype needs data the backend doesn't have, and set up a 15-minute chat instead of leaving a comment on a ticket.
actions: Present your team's work at the next show and tell, pitched at the non-technical people in the room.
Pair with a designer or user researcher for an afternoon.
obj: At show and tell I explained the API change in terms of what caseworkers would see, and the service owner said it was the first time it had clicked.
I committed to fixing a data bug before the client's board meeting, did it, and kept them updated daily. They now come to me directly with technical questions.
I spotted that the designer's prototype needed data we didn't hold, pulled in the data engineer early, and credited both of them in the sprint review.
I disagreed with the client's choice of reporting tool, checked with my tech lead how to raise it, and we presented the trade-offs together.

examples: Given a vague story to 'improve search', you list the open questions, agree a first small slice with the product manager, and ship it while the rest gets clarified.
You spot that a 'small tweak' touches three services and flag it at stand-up the same day, before it derails the sprint.
actions: Next time you pick up an unclear story, write down the open questions and agree a first slice before you start coding.
Raise any scope change at stand-up within a day of spotting it.
obj: Given a vague story to 'improve search', I listed the open questions, agreed a first slice with the product manager and shipped that while the rest was clarified.
I broke a messy data migration into five smaller steps with the team, delivered the first two, and asked the tech lead for help with the risky third.
When a 'small tweak' turned out to touch three services, I raised it at stand-up that day and we moved the deadline by a sprint rather than rushing it.
I recognised a caching problem I'd fixed on a previous project and applied the same approach, which saved the team about a week.
I explained to a newer engineer how our API work supports the council's goal of reducing phone calls, so they could prioritise sensibly.

examples: You notice response times creeping up before a benefits deadline, find the slow query, and propose a fix and a load test before users feel it.
actions: Set up or improve an alert on one key service metric for your project.
Run a load test on your service and share what you'd change.
obj: I set up health checks and dashboards across all five services before go-live, so we could see and fix problems before users reported them.
I introduced a checklist for deployments and incident handling, and got the team to use it consistently. Failed releases dropped noticeably.
Load testing showed the service would struggle at the benefits deadline, so I made the case for scaling the database and got it done in time.
When error rates spiked after a release, I rolled back, found the cause and wrote up what we'd change, all within the same afternoon.
In design reviews I suggested well-architected improvements such as autoscaling and retries, and two were adopted.

examples: You help your team make the repo ready to be coded in the open, walking a junior colleague through what that involves and why it matters.
actions: Pick one point of the Technology Code of Practice and show your team how your project meets it.
Pair with a junior engineer on applying a standard, such as accessibility or open code, to their story.
obj: I led the work to make our repo ready to code in the open and paired with a junior engineer so she could do the next one herself.

examples: You run a one-day spike with the designer, building two throwaway prototypes to test with users before the team commits to an approach.
actions: Suggest and run a time-boxed spike on your team's riskiest assumption.
Try a prototyping method you haven't used before and share what you learned.
obj: I ran a one-day spike with the designer and researcher to test two approaches with users, instead of prototyping on my own.
I turned our prototype components into a small reusable pattern library and refined it after each round of user testing.
I used a paper prototype for an early workflow idea and a coded prototype for the tricky interactions, choosing each for what we needed to learn.

examples: In sprint planning you push back on a feature request by pointing to what users said in research, and suggest a smaller change that meets the real need.
actions: Observe two user research sessions this quarter and share one insight at stand-up.
Add a 'user need' line to the next three stories you refine.
obj: I joined four user research sessions and worked with the researcher to make sure technical constraints were understood before we wrote stories.
When the client asked for a dashboard, I pointed to research showing users actually needed a weekly email, and we built that instead.
I pushed for research with screen reader users, which uncovered two blockers we fixed before launch.
I helped the team agree how we'd validate each story with users, and coached a junior engineer on writing user-focused acceptance criteria.
I recommended moving from ad-hoc surveys to short moderated sessions for technical features, which gave us much clearer answers.

examples: You write up a tricky database migration on the internal wiki, so colleagues know what you learned and when to bring you in.
actions: Write up something you've learned on a project and share it with your practice.
Ask two colleagues for targeted feedback on one skill you're building.
obj: I asked my tech lead and a senior engineer for specific feedback on my system designs, and changed how I document trade-offs as a result.
Knowing security was a gap, I paired with our security specialist for a sprint and ran my first threat model with her support.
I wrote up our database migration approach on the wiki and presented it at the engineering show and tell, and two teams have since asked me to help.
I ran a lunch-and-learn on contract testing and shared a starter template the practice now uses on new projects.
